etymologies.etymologyHTML: Borrowed from Latin sēdūcō (“to lead apart or astray”), from sē- (“aside, away, astray”) + dūcō (“to lead”); see duct. Compare adduce, conduce, deduce, etc. and Middle English seduct.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To beguile or lure (someone) away from duty, accepted principles, or proper conduct; to lead astray. [1520s[1]]

quote.citation: 1726 October 28, [Jonathan Swift], “The Author’s Oeconomy and Happy Life among the Houyhnhnms. […]”, in Travels into Several Remote Nations of the World.  […]  [Gulliver’s Travels], volume II, London:  […]  Benj[amin] Motte, […], →OCLC, part IV (A Voyage to the Houyhnhnms), page 308:
quote.text: […]  they alledged, That becauſe I had ſome Rudiments of Reaſon, added to the natural pravity of thoſe Animals, it was to be feared, I might be able to ſeduce them into the woody and mountainous parts of the Country, and bring them in Troops by night to deſtroy the Houyhnhnms Cattle, as being naturally of the ravenous kind, and averſe from Labour.

quote.citation: 1983, Lawrence Kasdan, George Lucas, Star Wars Episode VI: Return of the Jedi:
quote.text: Your father was seduced by the dark side of The Force.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To entice or induce (someone) to engage in a sexual relationship. [1550s[1]]

quote.citation: 1967, Calder Willingham, Buck Henry, The Graduate:
quote.text: "Mrs. Robinson, are you trying to seduce me?""Do you want me to seduce you?"

definitions.definition: (by extension, transitive, euphemistic) To have sexual intercourse with.
